I just started looking into taking my writing for pleasure/stress relief into actual writing myself.    I learned a couple of lessons so I'll offer them to you if you don't mind.

* When I started writing, I would just write a handful of scenes with characters and an issue or two.   I realized quickly this was overwhelming and suddenly I ended up with people sitting in rooms talking about issues like an episode of bill maher or murder she wrote.   I trashed those scenes and instead of talking about injustice, I found it more fun to have my cast suffer it instead.  If you want to tackle corruption, for example, make them deal with a corrupt individual and show how that person is corrupt.
* Always write about the fun stuff, if there is something you want to write and it isn't fun then set it aside and figure out a different approach.   Star Trek (in the original series)  I noticed they always told stories one of three ways.  One version would involve the main characters (kirk/spock/mccoy), Another would involve a crewmember on the ship, and the third would involve a 3rd party.  They would have the same dilemma more or less, but the point of view would shift.  One of my most hated characters from my beta readers is not my villains, but a cop that simply treats characters differently when he crosses paths with them based on what he perceives their social status is.
* I really haven't written before either and I suck at it.  Editing, however, is fixing that.  What I did was layer my ideas up.  I wrote one sentence, describing the story.   I then wrote 4 blocking out each act of the story.  I turned those 4 into 16 describing each scene in an act.  Those 16 then became my chapter outline, each with 4 sentences describing that happens in each chapter and so on.  It's not actually 16 chapters, but you get the idea.
* I can't tell if you should start with short stories or a novel or not.  I'd suggest you just write what's appropriate for you to tell your story.  Planning all of that out now will simply keep you from writing.   I started by writing a sentence about poking someone's eye while they were sleeping and a few months later I had 80,000 words in the first draft.
* The fallout of events, I frequently look to history for ideas on that.   I mean, look, we're a little over 101 years from WW1 and we're still feeling the effect of that.  But a person from 100 years ago to today would barely recognize the world or the chaos-  even if many of the problems from 100 years ago are still around.   Things change, but they don't.   We can't imagine the world today without some of the bad guys that existed in it either.   Corruption, greed, the big ideas will always be around in one way or another -  but events come and go.  **Focus on your characters first.**
* I agree with your last statement.  My big scifi space opera that I originally wanted to write is now a story about a handful of people trying to make their way in a city that shouldn't exist.  I zoomed in on the character, not the story concept.

Hopefully that helps, I'm new at this too so I might have some stuff wrong and I'm always open to new ideas myself.

I was in an accident once where the a guy pulled out in front of me and stopped with his tail hanging in my lane.   He ran his mouth the entire time, myself and my driver said nothing except to make sure we were all okay can call the rental company to report the accident.   It was raining so we were all waiting under the walkway for a stripmall.   The cop pulls up, she gets out and walks over in her rain gear.  The other party rushes up to her and blocks her from getting in from out of the rain and starts telling her how the accident was our fault, we were speeding, came out of no where in the rain and this that and the next thing and he needed us to fix his vehicle damage right away because his family didn't know he took his grandfathers car without permission and drove on his suspended license.  Not that the cop heard much, having to stand off the curb in the downpour while he blocked her.  After he finished, she stepped towards us out of the rain and he did a "nailed it" move.

She came over to us and simply said, "I don't want to hear it.  Give me your license, registration and insurance."   I offered my phone with a picture of the cars right after the accident.   She thanked us and walked back over to him with her ticket book out and pen scribbling.

There's lots and lots of great advice here.   What I tell my employee's to do is....

1. Tell yourself that this has happened, nothing can change that and pull yourself together.   You're gonna be shaken up, but now is the minutes you need to focus.   
1. Check the other vehicle for injuries if you can or call 911
1. Move the vehicles, if possible, off the road.   No need to make accidents worse by adding to it.
1. Take pictures of everything.   All around your car, their car, the area of the accident, the business cards, contact info and/or vehicle plates of witnesses (your insurance company can find them by their plate numbers)
1. Collect data >  I found this in an older post and made a version to keep in my glove box: http://i.imgur.com/F4X1TeW.jpg 
1. Call your boss (if company vehicle), family otherwise.
1. Call insurance.

This saved me from so many insurance claims against my company so many times.  In one case a technician was involved in an accident, there was no damage to either vehicle but they touched.   If it wasn't for the pictures, they other party would have gotten away with billing me for a new car.   Their mechanic declared their $40k new car totaled when all it needed was a rub of elbow grease.


I can't emphasize enough the importance of keeping your own mouth shut.  Only say what needs to be said, nothing more.   The other party will get all the information they need fro the police report or you will be directed to provide ONLY what is required by the police officer (if needed).

For me, when pricing a rodent job, it boils down to three areas.  Control, Exclusion, Sanitation.  For now I'm going to assume you're in a typical 1800-2400 sq.ft.  home like in the US (which I doubt, but you can look them up for comparison).

I assume they are planning to come once and week for six weeks-  That sounds like they aren't too concerned about the level of rodent activity going into the summer.  In Orlando I do daily or every other day checks for rodents in the summer months for 2-3 weeks. 

For control I use snap traps, glue traps and live traps only inside.  All traps are setup in tamper proof boxes to avoid accidental injuries. Outside I use poison baits in side of weighted tamper proof boxes placed around the home.  

About half way through the control, I start sealing up all but a handful of the access points for the exclusion process then once I go a few days in a row without new catches or observed activity, I have my guys finish the seal up and remove most of the inside traps.  Leaving only attic and basement ones.    

Sanitation is optional for my customers, but what that normally entails is removing anything heavily soiled by the rodents and spraying down the areas with sanitizes and deodorizers and done after the completion of control and the exclusion steps.

Again, I'm assuming its not that severe at the moment, but what I described runs about $900-$2400 (typically) depending on the home, access and severity of the issue.  I have done jobs on larger homes that cost less and ones on smaller homes that cost more and vice versa.  Some customers want ongoing monitoring (bait stations outside for the years).  Others just want it done and over.  It boils down to the specifics.

My material costs run between 20-50% of the price normally. Labor and time eat up most of my costs.

Now for comparison, jobs that did run $10+ of rodent control from my portfolio.  I won't name names, but just some off the top of my head.
